title: Count Occurrences
directAnswer: Scan once, incrementing a counter whenever `nums[i] == target`.

remember.takeaway: Counting means visiting every element — never break early.
remember.formula: c=0; for x: if x==target c++; return c
antiSignals: Sorted data — binary-search the first/last index instead

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums` and a `target`, return how many times `target` appears.
understanding: One pass with a counter incremented on each match.

approaches.name: Count matches
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Count how many times a value appears by scanning once and bumping a counter on every match. The key discipline: **don't stop at the first match** — counting requires visiting every element.

**Why no early exit.** Search returns on the first hit; counting must keep going to tally all of them. Breaking early is the classic copy-from-search bug.

**Why linear is optimal here.** For a single one-off query on unsorted data, you must examine each element, so O(n) is the floor. If you had to answer many count queries, you'd preprocess a frequency map once (O(n)) and then answer each query in O(1).

**On sorted data.** If the array were sorted, the matches form a contiguous block, so two binary searches (first and last position) count them in O(log n) — worth mentioning.

code.python:
def count(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for x in nums if x == target)
